newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Private pension plans on the rise in Latin America.
newsitem.headline: Private pension plans on the rise in Latin America.

text.p: Latin America's fledgling private pension plans are expanding rapidly and could capitalize as much as $100 billion by the end of the century, experts say.

After the introduction of private pension systems in five regional countries and the expected launching of similar plans in others next year, economists forecast a sharp upturn in funds bound for the capital markets and massive amounts of members.
In Latin America, Chile's is the best established system. Argentina, Peru, Colombia and Uruguay have introduced private pensions more recently.
Combined, these countries have private funds managing some $35 billion in funds for some 13.5 million members. Analysts say this figure could triple in the years to come.

"The private pensions systems, with obvious differences in every country, have spread widely and they have an important and significant future," said Walter Schultess, head of Argentina's private pensions watchdog, the SAFJP.

In January next year Mexico will introduce its own system and during 1997 possibly Bolivia, Guatemala and El Salvador will also launch private pensions, said specialists that met recently in Buenos Aires to discuss the Argentine model.

"The systems have produced a gigantic expansion of the integration of pension resources in Latin America's markets," said Jose Pinera, a Chilean economist and former labor minister under Gen. Augusto Pinochet's military rule.
Chile's system, often touted as the shining example of a Latin American pension system, was introduced during his term 15 years ago.

Nobel economist Gary Becker, who also attended the conference, said he cannot conceive of a world without private pension systems in the next century. The economist predicted a collapse of state pension systems, and said Europe and Asia would follow the lead taken by some Latin American nations.
Schulthess said he is permanently consulted about how the Argentine system works. He said he has had inquiries from Hungary, Spain, France, Britain, and even China.
British parliamentarians recently visited Chile and Argentina to study their systems.

"There is interest in the Argentine system firstly because it has been developed in a democratic system, something which is not too easy. Secondly, there is interest because of the cooperation between the state and the private funds," said Schulthess.
"I have been to a forum in Nicaragua and in all the Central American countries there is talk of reforms, with different emphasis, but a private system prevails," said Schulthess.
Pinera said the private pension structures "outside of the social welfare system will allow for more integration of the economies of Latin America."
Guillermo Alchouron, president of Origenes AFJP, Argentina's largest fund, said, "The model will grow in a significant fashion. The world has no other alternative system but the private one."
